state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine if you had a collection of toys, and you cut them all in half. Would the range of sizes stay the same?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Hmm, well if I cut them all in half, they'd all be smaller... so like, if one toy was 10 cm and another was 20 cm, after cutting they'd be 5 cm and 10 cm. Oh wait, the difference between them would still be the same wouldn't it? So maybe the range wouldn't change when you cut things in half?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine now if you had a collection of toys and you added 3 cm to each toy's height. Would the range of sizes stay the same?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher's approach leads the student to adopt an incorrect belief (that cutting in half preserves range), which is mathematically wrong and opposite to the student's initial correct answer, showing poor misconception engagement and domain accuracy.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses concrete, everyday analogies (a collection of toys) to help the student understand the abstract mathematical concept of range, which is a textbook example of the experiential strategy.
